questions.question: List the instruments of protection with their mechanisms, define dumping and infant industry, and explain why protection is described as politically easy but economically expensive.
questions.expected_answer: Tariffs: customs duties raising the import's shelf price, with revenue as a side payment. Quotas: quantity limits on imports — worse than tariffs because import licences become private prizes for favoured firms. Producer subsidies: grants or tax relief lowering home costs, protection hidden in the budget. Exchange control: rationing foreign currency so importers cannot pay abroad. Administrative and physical barriers: bans, standards enforced more zealously against foreign goods, deliberate red tape. Export incentives: the mirror image, helping home firms sell abroad. Dumping: exporting below cost or below the home price, often to bankrupt rivals before raising prices — met by anti-dumping duties, which South Africa applies (e.g. some imported chicken portions, steel). Infant industry: a young industry unable yet to match established foreign costs but plausibly able to once at scale — the textbook candidate for temporary shelter. Politically easy, economically expensive: every instrument raises prices or narrows choice for consumers, transferring from many consumers each paying slightly more to few producers and workers each gaining much — losses spread thinly and invisibly, gains concentrated and loud, so protection wins politics while costing the economy.

questions.question: Compare import substitution and export promotion as industrialisation strategies, and assess South Africa's experience of each.
questions.expected_answer: Import substitution — the inward road: replace imports with home production behind tariff walls; industry starts, jobs appear, imports fall and the home market is guaranteed. But walled industries stay small (the home market is the ceiling) and inefficient (no pressure to match world costs); foreign exchange drains into machinery for protected plants; consumers pay through higher prices. Apartheid South Africa ran this model with sanctions thickening the walls, building industries that struggled once opened. Export promotion — the outward road: export incentives and finance, cost-cutting infrastructure, skills, trade missions, funding tilted to exporters; the world market removes the ceiling so scale opens, world competition forces efficiency, and export earnings support the balance of payments — the East Asian route. Its conditions: export subsidies clash with world trade rules, success depends on working ports, rail and power, and the economy rides world demand swings. Democratic South Africa turned outward: steep tariff cuts through the 1990s, trade agreements, and sector master plans with the automotive programme as flagship (vehicles assembled and exported from the Eastern Cape and Gauteng), while clothing, poultry and steel remain contested protected files. The verdict: official policy backs export-led growth with selective protection, but the binding constraint is logistics and electricity rather than trade policy.

questions.question: Explain the rules of the world trading system and the four rungs of economic integration, using African examples, and give the honest four-part summary of globalisation.
questions.expected_answer: The line runs from GATT (1947) through eight tariff-cutting rounds to the WTO (1995, 160+ members including South Africa). Core rules: non-discrimination (most-favoured-nation — a benefit to one partner extends to all), national treatment (imports treated like local goods once inside), bound tariffs that cannot be raised at will, and dispute settlement through panels instead of retaliation. The result is trade liberalisation — tariffs a fraction of late-1940s levels, world trade multiplied — with standing critiques: rich countries still shield agriculture where developing countries hold advantage, the rules restrict industrial policies rich countries once used themselves, and gains divide unevenly. The ladder: free trade area — internal tariffs abolished, own external tariffs kept (AfCFTA, the world's largest by membership); customs union — adds a common external tariff (SACU, the world's oldest, revenue shared by formula); common market — adds free movement of labour and capital; economic union — adds harmonised policies and possibly one currency (the EU with the euro). South Africa stands on several rungs at once: SACU, SADC free trade, AfCFTA signatory. Honest summary: bigger markets and cheaper, better goods; real losers who deserve real help; and a rulebook that is imperfect and contested — yet better than no rules at all.
